name: Adonijah (son of Haggith)
title: The Ambitious Prince
summary: Adonijah was King David's fourth son, born to Haggith in Hebron. After his older brothers Amnon and Absalom had died, and the second son Daniel (Kileab) had disappeared from the biblical narrative, Adonijah stood as likely the oldest surviving heir to the throne. When David had grown old and weak, Adonijah took the initiative and attempted to secure the kingship with support from the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar. However, the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba prevented this by reminding David of his promise that Solomon would succeed him, and David immediately ordered Solomon's anointing. Adonijah sought refuge at the horns of the altar and was granted mercy by Solomon. After David's death, he asked to be given Abishag the Shunammite, David's last concubine, as a wife – a request that, according to the customs of that time, was interpreted as a renewed claim to the kingship. Solomon then had him executed. Adonijah's fate illustrates the brutal realities of ancient succession politics and underscores the biblical theme that God's choice does not necessarily follow human expectations regarding primogeniture.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah's Attempt to Seize the Throne
keyEvents.description: Adonijah exalted himself and declared he would become king while David was old and weak. He acquired chariots, horsemen, and fifty men who ran ahead of him—a method reminiscent of Absalom's earlier display of power. He gained support from the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar, and held a large sacrificial gathering at the Serpent Stone (Even ha-Zohelet) near En-Rogel.

keyEvents.title: Nathan and Bathsheba's Countermove
keyEvents.description: The prophet Nathan and Bathsheba went to King David and reminded him of his promise that Solomon would succeed him as king. David immediately ordered that Solomon be anointed as king.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah Seeks Refuge at the Altar
keyEvents.description: When Adonijah heard that Solomon had been anointed king, he fled in fear and grabbed hold of the altar's horns to seek protection. Solomon spared him on condition that he prove himself loyal and worthy.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah's Fatal Request for Abishag
keyEvents.description: After David's death, Adonijah approached Bathsheba and asked her to speak on his behalf with King Solomon to obtain Abishag of Shunem as his wife. In the ancient Near East, taking a king's concubine was regarded as a claim to the throne, and Solomon interpreted the request as a political power play.

keyEvents.title: Adonijah's Execution
keyEvents.description: King Solomon ordered Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, to execute Adonijah because of his request for Abishag. Solomon considered this high treason and a renewed claim to royal authority, and swore by the Lord that Adonijah must pay with his life.

versions.summary: Adonijah was the fourth son of King David and Haggith. He attempted to seize the throne before his father died but was passed over in favor of his younger half-brother Solomon. His later attempt to gain power through marriage led to his execution.
versions.title: The Ambitious Prince
versions.reason: [critical] The role is set to 'princess' (female), but Adonja was a male prince. The correct role should be 'prince'. Additionally, more roles can be added for completeness, such as 'throne pretender'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could be improved with a bit more context about the political dynamics and Adonja's position as the eldest surviving son after the deaths of Amnon and Absalom.; [minor] The list of siblings includes only some of David's sons. Daniel/Kileab (son of Abigail) is included, but for example Shephatiah and Ithream (2 Sam 3:4) are omitted. This is acceptable as a selection of the most well-known ones, but it could possibly be expanded.; [minor] The description says that Adonja 'declared himself king', but the text in 1 Kings 1:5 states more precisely that he 'exalted himself and said, "I will be king"'. He held a sacrificial gathering, but the formal declaration of kingship was more of a self-proclamation and preparation.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A profile like this should have footnotes on, among other things, the cultural significance of claiming a deceased king's concubine (the Abishag episode), the horns of the altar as a place of refuge, and the meaning of the name.

versions.summary: Adonijah was the fourth son of King David, born to Haggith. After the deaths of Amnon and Absalom, he was likely the oldest surviving heir, which may have strengthened his expectation of succession. When David was old and weak, Adonijah attempted to secure the throne with support from the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar. However, the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba intervened and had David anoint Solomon as king. Adonijah was granted mercy after seeking refuge at the altar, but his later request for Abishag of Shunem, David's former wife, to be given to him as a wife was interpreted by Solomon as a renewed claim to royal power, leading to his execution.
versions.title: The Ambitious Prince
versions.reason: [minor] The description mentions the 'Sohelet-stone' – this is an acceptable rendering, but the most common form in Norwegian is 'Serpent Stone' (Even ha-Sohelet). It may be helpful to include both terms for clarity.; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically sound. One possible improvement would be to clarify that Adonijah was David's fourth son by birth order (according to 2 Sam 3:2–4) and that he was likely the eldest surviving after both Amnon, and probably Daniel/Kilav, were out of the picture in addition to Absalom, thereby providing a more complete explanation for his expectations.; [minor] The final footnote notes that Daniel/Kilav is 'absent from the narratives', but could usefully expand by mentioning that some traditions suggest he died young or was unfit to rule, which further strengthens Adonijah's position.; [minor] The lifespan given as 'c. 1000–970 BC' is reasonable but somewhat short. David reigned c. 1010–970 BC. Adonijah was probably born early in David's reign in Hebron (2 Sam 3:4), so perhaps around 1005–1000 BC. The time of death shortly after David's death (c. 970 BC) is correct. The period could usefully be extended slightly, for example to 'c. 1005–970 BC'.

footnotes.text: The name Adonijah (Hebrew: אֲדֹנִיָּה, Adoniyyah) means 'my lord is Yahweh' or 'Yahweh is my lord'. It is a theophoric name containing the divine name and reflects a practice of piety among the Israelites in which children's names expressed trust in God.

In the ancient Near East, a king's harem was considered the king's property and a symbol of royal power. Demanding a deceased king's concubine or wife was interpreted as a claim to the throne. This pattern is well documented in biblical texts (cf. 2 Sam 3:7; 16:21-22) and other Near Eastern sources, explaining Solomon's strong reaction to Adonijah's request for Abishag of Shunem.

Grabbing hold of the altar's horns was a known practice for seeking asylum in ancient Israel. The altar served as a place of refuge (cf. Exod 21:13-14), but this right originally applied only to unintentional killings, not political treason. That Solomon nevertheless spared Adonijah shows a diplomatic approach in a politically sensitive situation.

En-Rogel (Hebrew: עֵין רֹגֵל), the place where Adonijah held his sacrificial gathering, was a spring southeast of Jerusalem near the confluence of the Hinnom and Kidron valleys. Archaeological investigations have identified this with Job's Well (Bir Ayyub) in present-day Jerusalem. The site had strategic significance as a meeting point outside the city walls.

Adonijah was likely the oldest surviving son of David after Amnon's murder (2 Sam 13) and Absalom's death (2 Sam 18). According to 2 Sam 3:2-4, David's order of sons was: Amnon, Daniel/Kileab, Absalom, Adonijah. The second son, Daniel/Kileab, is never mentioned again after the birth notice, which has led to rabbinic speculation that he died young or was unfit to rule.

The Stone of Zoheleth (Hebrew: אֶבֶן הַזֹּחֶלֶת, Even ha-Zohelet), often translated as 'the Serpent's Stone', was likely a well-known cultic or topographical marker near En-Rogel. The etymology of the name is disputed—it may mean 'sliding stone' or have an association with snakes. The choice of this location for Adonijah's sacrificial gathering may indicate it held ritual or political symbolic significance.

Rabbinic sources (Sanhedrin 21b) speculate that Daniel/Kileab received this double name because he 'humiliated' (Hebrew: kilam) his father by resembling his maternal grandfather Nabal more than David, or alternatively that he was so wise he did not need to study under David. His disappearance from the biblical narrative has given rise to many interpretations regarding his fate.
